messages.author: 673086e375eccf25
messages.subject: Using data with weights similar to the use in the standard glm function in R
parts:
I would like to analyse biologic responses with genotypes using the INLA package in R. My special intention is to include individuals, experiment days and
individual ages as random variables (using iid and random-walk models). The problem I have is that my genetic data contain an uncertainty parameter.
This means, that I have a table looking like this:

  Individual    Response (always the same)            Genotype        Probability (sum up to 1 per individual)    Age    Day of Experiment    Sex etc.
  1                0.3                                                    A                    0.2
  1                0.3                                                    B                    0.1
  1                0.3                                                    C                    0.8

With glm models in R, it is always possible to include the "Probability" in a "weights" vector for the observations.
Is there a similar way to do it with inla?

I have a similar problem with an association study, where I would like to include age as a random walk. How can I add "weights". I did not find
an answer in the FAQ or the documentation. But maybe there is a trick for that? Or can I write a likelihood function by myself which would include
weights?

Best regards from Lübeck,
Andreas

messages.author: 26c971075f8aedcc
messages.subject: Re: Using data with weights similar to the use in the standard glm function in R
parts:
Andreas,

On Dec 8, 2:17 pm, Andreas Recke <Andreas.Re...@uk-sh.de> wrote:
> ... The problem I have is that my genetic data contain an uncertainty parameter.

> This means, that I have a table looking like this:
>
>   Individual    Response (always the same)            Genotype
> Probability (sum up to 1 per individual)    Age    Day of Experiment    Sex
> etc.

> id y G Pr ...
>   1 0.3 A 0.2 ...
>   1 0.3 B 0.1 ...
>   1 0.3 C 0.8 ...

I reorganized the above table to understand your data. I guess the
last 0.8 needs to be 0.7. Are genotype levels A, B, and C actually
genotypes of one locus, e.g., A=AA, B=AB, and C=BB? If yes, then you
can not say that you have three y records per one individual. You have
one y record, but uncertainty in genotype. If you want to fit a model
to infer the effect of genotype on phenotype then you can fit it with
data being organized as:

id y GAA GAB GBB ...
1 0.3 0.2 0.1 0.7 --> uncertain genotype information
2 0.8 1.0 0.0 0.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype AA
3 0.9 0.0 1.0 0.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype AB
3 1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 --> this individual has certainly genotype BB

and in the model you simply have three covariates

y ~ GAA + GAB + GBB

where the estimate of regression coefficients of y on each G* would
represent genotype effects. If you are willing to assume only additive
effect at this locus you can do

GC <- with(mydata, GAA*0 + GAB*1 + GBB*2)

y ~ GC

where the estimate of regression coefficient of y on GC would be the
average allele substitution effect.

Regards, Gregor Gorjanc

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Using data with weights similar to the use in the standard glm function in R
parts:
yes, its the same. there is an argument 'weights' in inla() which is the
same argument as in 'glm'. however, its default disabled, to avoid
mis-usage:

> y = 1
> r = inla(y~1, data=data.frame(y), weights=2)
Error in inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y), weights = 2) :
Argument 'weights' must be enabled before use due to the risk of
mis-interpreting the results.
Use 'inla.setOption("enable.inla.argument.weights", TRUE)' to enable
it; see ?inla

messages.author: 26c971075f8aedcc
messages.subject: Re: Using data with weights similar to the use in the standard glm function in R
parts: Hi,

On Mar 14, 7:59 am, Finn Lindgren <finn.lindg...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
> I'm not sure if your question relates to this thread (if it does, perhaps
> Gregor has an answer) since you didn't specify exactly what you mean by
> "weighted observations".  There is another thread discussing using weighted
> log-likelihood-values.  Is that what you mean, or something different?

Bellow is a suggestion given to me from my colleague not that long ago
that might be useful for you with INLA if weights argument is causing
you troubles.

Regards, Gregor

consider yi=mu+zi'b + ei with var(ei)=s2i*varE

pre-multiply both sides of the equation using wi=1/sqrt(s2i) to get

wi*yi=wi*mu+wi*zi'b+ wi*ei

now, the var(wi*ei)=wi^2*s2i*varE=varE

Therfore, simply 'cheat' your program by giving wi*yi as phenotype,
xi*zi as markers and wi as a fixed effect, and run the model with
homogeneous residual variance.
